title: Abstract Algebra
body:
MATH 2101 studies a set together with an operation on it and a short list of rules that
operation obeys. Every theorem is proved from the rules alone, never from what the elements
are, so one proof holds at once for every system satisfying them. A result proved about groups
applies to the integers under addition, to the symmetries of a triangle, to invertible
matrices, and to the points on an elliptic curve, because all four satisfy the same four
axioms.

The structures stack in one direction. A [[Group]] has one operation, a [[Ring]] has two, and
a [[Field]] is a ring where division works, and each added requirement produces a chapter of
consequences. The course opens concretely with the [[Integer|integers]] and
[[Modular Arithmetic]], because $\mathbb{Z}$ is the example every later abstraction is
modelled on, and it closes on [[Finite Field|finite fields]], where the abstraction becomes
something a machine computes with directly.

[[CRYPTOGRAPHY]] (MATH 4111) lists this course as its prerequisite and spends a term using the
groups, rings and fields built here. The [[Cyclic Group]] structure of the [[Roots of Unity]]
is what the [[Discrete Fourier Transform]] is assembled from in
[[FOURIER AND COMPLEX ANALYSIS]], and $GF(2^8)$ is why arithmetic on a [[Byte]] forms a field.

## Topics

### Arithmetic where the numbers wrap

[[Modular Arithmetic]] is the concrete starting point. Working modulo $n$ means treating two
integers as the same when they differ by a multiple of $n$, written
$a \equiv b \pmod n$, which holds exactly when $n \mid (a-b)$.

```
mod 6:  ...  -6 ≡ 0,  7 ≡ 1,  13 ≡ 1,  20 ≡ 2  ...

the six classes are [0] [1] [2] [3] [4] [5], and arithmetic acts on classes:
   [4] + [5] = [9] = [3]        [4] × [5] = [20] = [2]
```

The shift that makes this algebra is that $[4]$ stops being a leftover from a division and
becomes an object in its own right, one of the six elements of $\mathbb{Z}_6$. Congruence
survives addition and multiplication, so reducing at any point in a calculation is legal,
which is what keeps modular exponentiation from overflowing. Congruence does not survive
cancellation: $2 \times 3 \equiv 2 \times 0 \pmod 6$ while $3 \not\equiv 0$.

Division works only sometimes, and the condition is exact. A class $[a]$ has a multiplicative
inverse in $\mathbb{Z}_n$ exactly when $\gcd(a,n) = 1$. In $\mathbb{Z}_6$ only $[1]$ and $[5]$
are invertible, and in $\mathbb{Z}_5$ every non-zero class is, which is the first sign that a
prime modulus behaves differently.

### Euclid's algorithm, and how to invert

The [[Euclidean Algorithm]] computes a gcd by repeated division, in $O(\log \min(a,b))$ steps,
with consecutive Fibonacci numbers as the worst case. Running it backwards produces Bézout's
identity, $\gcd(a,b) = ax + by$, and that is what inverts an element:

```
invert 7 mod 26:

  26 = 3(7) + 5          forward: the gcd is 1
   7 = 1(5) + 2
   5 = 2(2) + 1

  1 = 5 - 2(2)           backward: substitute each remainder
    = 5 - 2(7 - 5)      = 3(5) - 2(7)
    = 3(26 - 3·7) - 2(7) = 3(26) - 11(7)

  so  -11(7) ≡ 1 (mod 26),  and  -11 ≡ 15,  so  7⁻¹ = 15
  check: 7 × 15 = 105 = 4(26) + 1  ✓
```

That computation is the whole of RSA key generation, performed on numbers hundreds of digits
long. [[GCD and LCM]] holds the implementation while this course holds the proof and the
termination argument, and [[Division Algorithm]] and [[Prime Number]] are the first-year notes
underneath, reread here with the gcd as a generator and primality as irreducibility.

### Groups

A [[Group]] is a set $G$ with one operation satisfying four axioms:

```
closure         a, b in G  =>  a·b in G
associativity   (a·b)·c = a·(b·c)
identity        there is an e with e·a = a·e = a
inverses        every a has an a⁻¹ with a·a⁻¹ = e
```

Commutativity is not on the list, and a group that has it is called abelian. Leaving it off is
deliberate, since function composition and matrix multiplication are the motivating examples
and neither commutes.

From those four axioms alone, the identity is unique, every inverse is unique, cancellation
holds, and $(ab)^{-1} = b^{-1}a^{-1}$ with the order reversed. Nothing about what the elements
are was used, which is the point of the exercise.

The word order carries two meanings that stay separate for the rest of the course. The order
of a group is $|G|$, its number of elements. The order of an element $a$ is the smallest
$k > 0$ with $a^k = e$.

A [[Subgroup]] is a subset that is itself a group under the same operation, and the one-step
test replaces rechecking all four axioms with checking non-emptiness plus closure under the
operation and under inverses. For a finite subset, closure alone suffices, because repeatedly
applying a finite set's operation must eventually return the identity.

### Cyclic groups

A [[Cyclic Group]] is generated by a single element, meaning every member is a power of one
element $g$.

```
Z₆ under addition, generated by 1:  1, 1+1=2, 3, 4, 5, 0     all six
generated by 2:                     2, 4, 0                   only three
```

The subgroup $\{0, 2, 4\}$ is what $2$ generates, and its size divides 6. In general $g^k$
generates the whole group of order $n$ exactly when $\gcd(k,n) = 1$, which is why $1$ and $5$
are the generators of $\mathbb{Z}_6$ and $2$, $3$ and $4$ are not.

Every cyclic group is abelian, and up to [[Isomorphism]] there are only two, $\mathbb{Z}$ and
$\mathbb{Z}_n$, so classifying cyclic groups is finished. Plenty of abelian groups fall
outside the class. The $n$th [[Roots of Unity]] form a cyclic group of order $n$ under
multiplication, where multiplying adds angles and wraps, which is $\mathbb{Z}_n$ drawn on the
unit circle.

### Permutations and symmetry

[[Permutation Group]] covers the concrete groups, and by Cayley's theorem also the general
case, since every finite group is isomorphic to a subgroup of some symmetric group. A
permutation is written in cycle notation, and every permutation factors into disjoint cycles:

```
(1 2 3)(4 5)     sends 1→2→3→1 and 4→5→4

order = lcm(3, 2) = 6      applying it six times returns everything home
```

Parity is well defined: every decomposition of a permutation into transpositions has the same
parity, and a $k$-cycle is even exactly when $k$ is odd. The [[Symmetric Group]] $S_n$ contains
all $n!$ permutations, the [[Alternating Group]] $A_n$ contains the even half with order
$n!/2$, and the [[Dihedral Group]] $D_n$ contains the $2n$ symmetries of a regular $n$-gon.

$D_3$ is the example to keep at hand, the six symmetries of a triangle, generated by a
rotation $r$ and a reflection $s$ with $srs = r^{-1}$. That relation is non-commutativity
written as an equation: reflecting, rotating and reflecting again runs the rotation backwards.
$S_3 = D_3$ is the smallest non-abelian group, with six elements.

### Cosets and Lagrange's theorem

A [[Coset]] shifts a subgroup around the group. Taking $H = \{0, 2, 4\}$ inside
$\mathbb{Z}_6$:

```
0 + H = {0, 2, 4}
1 + H = {1, 3, 5}
2 + H = {2, 4, 0}   the same set as 0 + H
```

Every coset has the same size as $H$, any two are either identical or disjoint, and together
they cover the group. Those three facts partition $G$ into equal blocks, and counting the
blocks gives [[Lagrange's Theorem]]:

$$
|G| = [G:H] \cdot |H|, \quad\text{so } |H| \text{ divides } |G|
$$

Here $6 = 2 \times 3$. The converse fails, since $A_4$ has order 12 and no subgroup of order 6.

The corollaries carry the weight. The order of every element divides $|G|$, so $a^{|G|} = e$
for every $a$ in the group. Every group of prime order is cyclic and has no non-trivial
subgroups, because no number other than 1 and $p$ divides $p$. Applying $a^{|G|} = e$ to the
group of units mod $p$, which has $p-1$ elements, gives Fermat's little theorem,
$a^{p-1} \equiv 1 \pmod p$. A structural result about cosets has become the arithmetic RSA
decryption relies on.

### Maps between structures

A [[Homomorphism]] preserves the operation, satisfying
$\varphi(ab) = \varphi(a)\varphi(b)$, and is permitted to lose information. The determinant is
one, sending matrix multiplication to number multiplication, and the sign of a permutation is
another, sending composition to multiplication in $\{1,-1\}$. A homomorphism is injective
exactly when its kernel is trivial, which is the group version of the same statement in
[[Kernel and Range]].

An [[Isomorphism]] loses nothing, so two isomorphic groups are one object under different
labels and every group-theoretic statement transfers. The harder skill is the reverse, proving
two groups are not isomorphic by finding an invariant they disagree on, such as being abelian,
the number of elements of order 2, or being cyclic.

### Rings

A [[Ring]] has two operations. It is an abelian group under addition, has an associative
multiplication, and multiplication distributes over addition. Commutativity of multiplication,
a multiplicative identity, and multiplicative inverses are each optional, and adding them back
one at a time gives the ladder from ring to commutative ring to integral domain to field.

A zero divisor is a non-zero $a$ with $ab = 0$ for some non-zero $b$. In $\mathbb{Z}_6$,
$2 \times 3 = 0$, so both are zero divisors, and their presence is exactly what breaks
cancellation. An integral domain has none. $\mathbb{Z}$ is an integral domain where division
fails, and that gap is where all of divisibility and factorisation lives.

Ideals are what a quotient is taken by, and $\mathbb{Z}/n\mathbb{Z} = \mathbb{Z}_n$ ties the
whole block back to the first section: the congruence classes of modular arithmetic are the
elements of a quotient ring.

### Polynomials

[[Polynomial Ring]] covers $F[x]$, polynomials with coefficients in a field, and the point of
the block is that it behaves almost exactly like $\mathbb{Z}$. Division with remainder works,
a Euclidean algorithm runs, factorisation into irreducibles is unique, and quotients exist.
Degrees add under multiplication, $(x-a)$ divides $f$ exactly when $f(a) = 0$, and a
degree-$n$ polynomial has at most $n$ roots.

[[Irreducibility]] is primality for polynomials, and the field it is stated over decides the
answer. $x^2+1$ is irreducible over $\mathbb{R}$, since no real number squares to $-1$, and it
factors as $(x+i)(x-i)$ over $\mathbb{C}$. The tests are Eisenstein's criterion, the rational
root theorem, and the shortcut for degree 2 or 3, where having no root in the field is enough
to conclude irreducibility. That shortcut fails from degree 4, where
$x^4 + 2x^2 + 1 = (x^2+1)^2$ has no real root and factors anyway.

### Fields and finite fields

A [[Field]] is a commutative ring in which every non-zero element has a multiplicative
inverse, which is two abelian groups carried on one set. $\mathbb{Z}_n$ is a field exactly
when $n$ is prime, because a composite $n = ab$ supplies the zero divisors above and a zero
divisor can have no inverse.

The characteristic is the number of times 1 must be added to itself to reach 0, and it is
always 0 or prime. In characteristic 2, $x + x = 0$, so addition is XOR and every element is
its own negative, which is why subtraction disappears from binary arithmetic.

[[Field Extension]] adjoins a root of an irreducible polynomial. The worked example is
$\mathbb{C} = \mathbb{R}[x]/(x^2+1)$: take polynomials over $\mathbb{R}$, declare $x^2+1$ to
be zero, and the symbol $x$ becomes a square root of $-1$. Every element is then $a + bx$,
which is a complex number written differently. The degree $[K:F]$ is the dimension of $K$ as a
[[Vector Space]] over $F$ and equals $\deg f$, so $[\mathbb{C}:\mathbb{R}] = 2$. In general
$F[x]/(f)$ is a field exactly when $f$ is irreducible, which is the polynomial version of
$\mathbb{Z}_p$ being a field.

[[Finite Field]] is where the course lands. A finite field has $p^n$ elements for a prime $p$,
and exactly one field exists of each prime power size, which is why $\mathbb{Z}_4$ fails to be
a field while $GF(4) = \mathbb{Z}_2[x]/(x^2+x+1)$ succeeds. The non-zero elements always form
a cyclic group of order $q-1$.

$GF(2^8)$ is the field a [[Byte]] lives in, and it is the payoff of the whole course:

```
a byte is a polynomial with 8 binary coefficients
   $53  =  01010011  =  x⁶ + x⁴ + x + 1

addition is XOR                    (characteristic 2, so no carries)
multiplication is polynomial multiply, reduced mod x⁸+x⁴+x³+x+1
```

Every non-zero byte has a multiplicative inverse there, which $\mathbb{Z}_{256}$ cannot
offer, since 256 is composite. AES and Reed-Solomon are both built on that fact.

## Related courses

- [[INTRODUCTION TO COMPUTER SCIENCE 2]] (COMP 1633) implements the number theory, with
  [[Division Algorithm]] as `/` and `%`, [[GCD and LCM]] as Euclid in a loop, and
  [[Prime Number]] as trial division. This course supplies the reason each one is correct.
- [[DISCRETE MATH]] (MATH 1271) is the middle rung, supplying [[Proof]],
  [[Proof By Induction]] and [[Sets]]. Watch the shared word: [[Permutation]] there is the
  count $P(n,r)$, and [[Permutation Group]] here is an object, with $n!$ as the place the two
  meet.
- [[LINEAR ALGEBRA]] (MATH 1203) states [[Vector Space]] as a bare axiom list in the same
  style, and a vector space is defined over a field, so [[Field]] completes that definition.
  [[Complex Numbers]] there is $\mathbb{R}$ with a root of $x^2+1$ adjoined here, the
  [[Determinant]] is a [[Homomorphism]], and [[Kernel and Range]] is the same theorem as
  kernel and image.
- [[CRYPTOGRAPHY]] (MATH 4111) has this course as its stated prerequisite. RSA is
  [[Modular Arithmetic]] with Fermat's theorem and [[Euclidean Algorithm|modular inversion]],
  AES is arithmetic in $GF(2^8)$, Diffie-Hellman is the discrete logarithm in a
  [[Cyclic Group]], and elliptic curves carry a group law over a [[Finite Field]].
- [[FOURIER AND COMPLEX ANALYSIS]] (MATH 4199) is where the [[Cyclic Group]] pays off outside
  algebra. The [[Roots of Unity]] form one, the [[Discrete Fourier Transform]] matrix is built
  from powers of a single generator, and the [[Fast Fourier Transform]] halving step passes to
  the subgroup of order $n/2$.
- [[COMPUTING MACHINERY]] (COMP 2655) and [[COMPUTING MACHINERY 2]] (COMP 2659) run this
  algebra in hardware without naming it. [[Integer Representation]] and [[Complements]] are
  arithmetic in $\mathbb{Z}_{2^n}$, so unsigned overflow is reduction behaving correctly.
  [[Boolean Algebra]] is $GF(2)$ from the circuit side, and the parity bit in
  [[Error Detection]] is a linear equation over it.
- [[INFORMATION STRUCTURES]] (COMP 2631) uses $\mathbb{Z}_n$ on every hash, since
  [[Hashing]] and the [[Hash Function]] map a key to a congruence class, and the advice to use
  a prime table size is this course's theorem about $\mathbb{Z}_p$.
- [[ALGORITHMS AND COMPLEXITY]] takes the [[Euclidean Algorithm]] as its canonical
  logarithmic algorithm, and $|S_n| = n!$ as the reason brute force over orderings fails.
- [[INTRODUCTION TO COMPUTABILITY]] (COMP 2613) uses the idea behind [[Isomorphism]] when
  [[Simulation]] has one machine imitate another.
- [[THE NEW TURING OMNIBUS]] holds [[Error Correcting Code]], which applies finite field
  theory. Reed-Solomon treats a block of bytes as a polynomial over $GF(2^8)$, and the
  at-most-$n$-roots fact from [[Polynomial Ring]] is why the redundancy recovers the data.
